r: A pace plan treats the body as an engine that runs at a fixed output, but the body actually runs on a fuel tank. A trained runner stores roughly 400 to 500 grams of glycogen in the muscles and liver, which covers about 2,000 calories. Marathon pace burns close to 100 calories per mile, so that reserve runs out somewhere near mile 20. After that, the body has to rely on fat oxidation, which delivers ATP more slowly. Suppose a runner gained a few seconds early on a cool, flat first half. That runner now finds the fuel account overdrawn. Splits that looked sustainable at mile 12 demand more power than the body can release from its fuel. Heat, dehydration that costs two percent of body mass, and eccentric damage to the quads all deepen the deficit. Then the wall arrives. To prevent it, run the second half faster than the first, take in 60 to 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, and do long runs that train the body to burn fat before race day.
